_README: Hand-written for this project. NOT adapted from the purchased outlines, and
not from the BSB — only the section headings come from there.
Drawn from plain historical fact and public-domain reference works (Matthew
Henry's Commentary, 1710; the Scofield Reference Bible, 1909).
Shipped under DATA_PROFILE=public. Add books freely — a book with no entry
here simply renders without an introduction.
Voice: for someone about to read the book who may never have read it before.
Say what it is, when it was written, what it is doing, and what a reader will
actually meet in it. No exhortation, no selling. Two short paragraphs.
PROVENANCE: every intro records who drafted it and what they had been exposed
to. See _provenance below and src/data/sections/SOURCE.md. Eight books are
reserved for the owner because an assistant had already read the purchased
introductions for them in the session where the PDFs were ingested, and a
no-shared-sentence check cannot detect borrowed structure or emphasis.

ruth:
Ruth is four chapters long and set during the time of the judges, a period the book of Judges describes as lawless and grim. It opens with a famine, a family leaving Bethlehem for Moab, and three deaths in quick succession — and then narrows to two widows walking back to Bethlehem with nothing. Ruth, the younger, is a Moabitess, a foreigner from a people Israel had every historical reason to distrust.

What follows is an ordinary story: gleaning in a barley field, a landowner's kindness, a legal transaction at the town gate about who has the right to redeem a dead man's property and marry his widow. It is told without miracles and almost without mention of God acting directly. The last five verses reveal why it was kept: Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David. In Jewish tradition it is read at Shavuot, the festival of the harvest it describes.
jonah:
Jonah is the odd one out among the prophets. The other prophetic books are collections of oracles — what the prophet said. Jonah is a story about the prophet himself, and he comes off badly in nearly all of it. Four short chapters: a commission refused, a storm, a fish, a reluctant sermon, and an argument with God that the book simply stops in the middle of.

Jonah is named in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet under Jeroboam II, which places him in the eighth century BC. Nineveh was the great city of Assyria — the empire that would destroy the northern kingdom within his century — so his refusal to go is not cowardice so much as a refusal to see that city spared. That is what the closing chapter is about, and it ends on a question God asks Jonah, which the book never answers. The reader is left holding it.
ecclesiastes:
Ecclesiastes is the most unguarded book in the Bible. Its speaker calls himself Qoheleth — usually rendered "the Preacher" or "the Teacher" — and he has tried everything: work, pleasure, learning, building, wealth. His verdict on all of it is the word the King James translates "vanity", which in Hebrew is *hevel*: vapour, breath, something you cannot get hold of. He uses it nearly forty times.

It belongs to the wisdom literature, alongside Proverbs and Job, and it argues with Proverbs more than it agrees. Where Proverbs says the diligent prosper, Ecclesiastes notes that the same fate meets the wise and the fool, and that a man's heirs may squander everything he built. It does not resolve this. Readers have found it bleak and readers have found it the only honest book they own; both are reading it correctly. It ends by telling you to fear God and keep his commandments, having spent twelve chapters refusing to pretend that this makes life legible.
philippians:
Paul wrote Philippians from prison, probably in Rome in the early 60s AD, to a church he had founded himself about ten years earlier. Acts 16 tells that founding: a riverside prayer meeting, a businesswoman named Lydia, a girl delivered from a spirit of divination, and a night in the Philippian jail that ended with the jailer baptised. Philippi was a Roman colony, and its Christians were the first in Europe.

The letter is warm in a way Paul's letters often are not. He is not correcting a crisis here; he is thanking them for money they sent, explaining his situation, and asking them to stop quarrelling — two women are named. Chapter two carries what is probably an early Christian hymn about Christ emptying himself, quoted rather than composed for the occasion. Paul writes repeatedly about joy, from a cell, without explaining the contradiction.
james:
James reads less like a letter than like the wisdom books of the Old Testament — short, blunt, practical, moving quickly between subjects without connecting them. It has more imperatives per line than anything else in the New Testament. The author is traditionally identified as James the brother of Jesus, who led the Jerusalem church and is named in Acts 15 presiding over the council there.

Its concerns are consistent: what people do with money, what they do with their tongues, and how they treat the poor when nobody is watching. The passage on faith and works in chapter two has been argued over since the Reformation, when Luther called the book an epistle of straw for it. Read next to Paul it looks like a contradiction; read on its own terms it is asking a narrower question — not how a person is saved, but how you would tell.
exodus:
Exodus picks up about four hundred years after Genesis ends, with Joseph's family grown into a people and enslaved by a Pharaoh who "knew not Joseph". It covers two things: a rescue, and what the rescued were then asked to become. The first half is the famous half — the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover, the sea opening — and it moves fast.

The second half slows to a halt, and readers often stop there. After Sinai the book turns to law and then to architecture: the Ten Commandments, then chapters of case law, then detailed specifications for a portable tent and its furnishings, given once as instruction and repeated almost verbatim as a record that it was built. The repetition is the point. A people who had just been property are given, in exhaustive detail, something of their own to make.
leviticus:
Leviticus is the book most reading plans die in. It is almost entirely instruction — sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, festivals, land — delivered with little narrative to carry a reader along. Its two stories are both brief and both grim.

It rewards being read as a manual for a particular people at a particular moment: newly freed, camped around a tent, working out what it means that God is living in the middle of them. Nearly everything in it turns on that one problem. The word "holy" appears more here than anywhere else in the Bible, and it means set apart rather than morally superior. Chapter 19 is the one most readers know without knowing where it is from: love thy neighbour as thyself, sitting in the middle of rules about harvesting and wages and not cursing the deaf.
numbers:
Numbers takes its English name from the two censuses that open and close it — one generation counted at Sinai, another counted forty years later on the plains of Moab. Almost everyone in the first list dies before the second. That is the book's argument in its structure: this is what happened to the generation that came out of Egypt.

What fills the space between is the wilderness, and it is mostly complaint. Food, water, leadership, the report of the spies who said the land could not be taken. Twelve went in, two came back willing. Numbers also holds some of the strangest material in the Old Testament — a bronze serpent, a talking donkey, a foreign prophet hired to curse Israel who blesses it instead — and one of its most familiar passages, the blessing of chapter 6: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee.
deuteronomy:
Deuteronomy is one long farewell. Moses is a hundred and twenty years old, standing east of the Jordan with a people he will not cross it with, and the book is essentially three sermons and a song. Its name means "second law" — it retells and reapplies what was given at Sinai, to a generation that was not there.

It is the most quoted Old Testament book in the New. The Shema is here — hear, O Israel, the LORD our God is one LORD — and so is the command to love God with all your heart, which Jesus calls the first commandment. Jesus answers all three wilderness temptations with lines from it. The book ends with Moses seeing the land from Mount Nebo and dying there, and the note that no one knows where he is buried.
joshua:
Joshua covers a single generation and one task: crossing into the land and taking it. The first half is campaign — Jericho, Ai, a long day at Gibeon — and the second half is surveying, dividing the territory tribe by tribe with the precision of a land registry.

It is the book modern readers most often find hard, and it is worth knowing that going in rather than being surprised by it. The conquest accounts are written in the idiom of ancient war reporting, sweeping and total in their language, and the same book that says a region was wholly taken later describes the people still living there. Its closing scene is the one most often remembered: Joshua, old, gathering the tribes at Shechem and making them choose out loud — as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
judges:
Judges covers roughly three centuries between Joshua's death and the first king, and it gets darker as it goes. The pattern repeats: the people drift, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, God raises up a deliverer — a "judge", meaning a military leader rather than a magistrate — and there is peace until that judge dies. Then it begins again, worse.

The judges themselves are an uneven collection: Deborah, who governs and goes to war; Gideon, who needs three signs before he will believe; Jephthah, who makes a vow that costs him his daughter; Samson, who is more a force of nature than a leader. The last chapters abandon the pattern for two atrocities told without comment, and the book's final sentence is its verdict on the whole period: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
1-samuel:
First Samuel is about the arrival of kingship and what it cost. It opens with a barren woman praying at the tabernacle and closes with a king dead on a battlefield, and it turns on three figures: Samuel, the last of the judges; Saul, the first king; and David, the shepherd anointed while Saul still reigns.

The people ask for a king so they can be like the other nations, and Samuel warns them at length what a king will take. They ask anyway. Saul begins well and unravels, and much of the second half is a long pursuit — Saul hunting David through the wilderness while David, twice able to kill him, does not. The famous scenes are here: the boy hearing his name in the night, the anointing of the youngest son nobody thought to call in from the sheep, and David and Goliath.
2-samuel:
Second Samuel is David's reign, and it divides cleanly at chapter 11. Before it, almost everything goes right: the tribes united, Jerusalem taken and made the capital, the ark brought up with David dancing before it, and a promise that his house and kingdom will be established for ever.

After it, almost nothing does. The adultery with Bathsheba and the arranged death of her husband are told plainly, with none of the softening a court history would normally apply to its own king, and the consequences run through the rest of the book: a child's death, a daughter raped, a son murdered, and finally Absalom's rebellion and David fleeing his own city barefoot. The book is remarkable partly for what it refuses to hide about the man it plainly admires.
1-kings:
First Kings opens with Solomon, and the early chapters are the high-water mark of the whole Old Testament story: a young king asking for wisdom rather than wealth, the temple built and filled, a foreign queen coming to see whether the reports are true. Then the same king accumulates wives, horses and foreign altars, and the account turns cold.

After his death the kingdom splits — ten tribes north under Jeroboam, two south under Rehoboam — and the book settles into a rhythm of paired reigns, each king given a short verdict on whether he did right or evil. Into that comes Elijah, and the pace changes entirely: the drought, the ravens, the widow's jar of meal, the confrontation on Carmel, and then the collapse afterwards in the desert, where God is not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire but in a still small voice.
2-kings:
Second Kings carries the two kingdoms to their ends. It opens with Elijah taken up in a whirlwind and Elisha asking for a double portion of his spirit, and the Elisha chapters that follow hold some of the most domestic miracles in scripture — a borrowed axe head, a poisoned pot of stew, oil that keeps pouring while there are jars to fill.

Then the record grinds on through the kings, and the verdicts get worse. Samaria falls to Assyria in 722 BC and the northern kingdom simply stops. Judah lasts another century and a half, with two genuine reforms under Hezekiah and Josiah, before Babylon comes. The book ends with Jerusalem burned, the temple stripped, the people deported, and a last small note: the exiled king of Judah released from prison in Babylon and given a seat at the table. It is not resolution, but it is not nothing.
1-chronicles:
First Chronicles retells material a reader has already met in Samuel and Kings, and the interesting question is what it leaves out. It was compiled after the exile, for people who had come back to a ruined city and needed to know whether they were still the same nation. The first nine chapters are genealogy — from Adam forward — and they are there to answer exactly that.

The rest is David, but a narrower David than the one in Second Samuel. Bathsheba is absent. So is Absalom's rebellion, and the long decline. What the Chronicler keeps is the ark brought to Jerusalem, the organisation of the Levites and the singers, and David spending his last years gathering materials and drawing plans for a temple he is told he will not build. The book ends with him handing those plans to Solomon in front of the whole assembly.
2-chronicles:
Second Chronicles runs from Solomon's temple to the fall of Jerusalem, and then adds four verses that change the ending. It follows the kings of Judah only; the northern kingdom appears when it intersects with the south and is otherwise left to Kings. The temple is the organising interest throughout — built, filled, neglected, plundered, repaired, cleansed, and finally burned.

Its best-known passages are the reform narratives, where a king reopens the doors his father shut: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah keeping a Passover so late that the northern remnant is invited to it, and Josiah finding the book of the law during building work. The ending is the reason the Hebrew Bible places Chronicles last. Jerusalem falls, the land lies desolate for seventy years, and then Cyrus of Persia issues a decree — and the book stops mid-proclamation, on the word "go up".
ezra:
Ezra begins where Chronicles stops, with the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC, and covers two returns from Babylon separated by about eighty years. The first, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, rebuilds the altar and lays a foundation; the work then halts for years under local opposition and imperial correspondence, and resumes only when Haggai and Zechariah start preaching. The second temple is finished in 516 BC.

Ezra himself does not appear until chapter seven. He is a scribe, expert in the law of Moses, and he arrives with a royal commission and a second group of returnees. Some of the book is in Aramaic rather than Hebrew — the language of Persian administration, used for the documents it quotes. It ends abruptly and unhappily, with Ezra confronting intermarriage among the returned community, and a list of names. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are a single book.
nehemiah:
Nehemiah is written largely in the first person, which makes it unusual. Its author is cupbearer to Artaxerxes in the Persian capital when news reaches him that Jerusalem's wall is still broken down a century after the first return. He asks for leave, gets it, and the book becomes an account of a building project conducted under harassment — night inspections, work rotas, families assigned to the section of wall nearest their own houses, and a standing guard.

The wall takes fifty-two days. Then the book changes character: Ezra reads the law aloud from a wooden platform at the Water Gate from morning until midday, with Levites moving through the crowd explaining it, and the people weep. What follows is a covenant signed by name, a repopulating of the city, and Nehemiah's second term, in which he returns to find the reforms lapsed and deals with it bluntly. The last verse is a request that God remember him.
esther:
Esther never mentions God. It is the only book in the Hebrew Bible that does not, and readers have argued about that for two thousand years. It is set entirely in the Persian empire, in the citadel of Susa, in the reign of Ahasuerus — the king the Greeks called Xerxes — and it reads like court history: banquets, protocol, insomnia, and the exact wording of edicts that cannot be revoked once sealed.

The plot turns on reversals. A queen is deposed for refusing to appear and a Jewish orphan takes her place without disclosing who she is. Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai and is hanged on it. A decree to destroy the Jews on a date chosen by lot is answered by a second decree permitting them to defend themselves. The feast of Purim takes its name from that lot, and Esther is read aloud at it each year, in full, with the congregation drowning out Haman's name.
job:
Job is a poem with a story wrapped around it. The prose opening and closing are plain and quick; everything between chapters three and forty-two is verse, and it is some of the most difficult Hebrew in the Bible. Job is not an Israelite and the land of Uz is not in Israel. No covenant, no temple, no law — the book is deliberately set outside all of that.

The question is not whether Job sinned. The reader is told in the first chapter that he did not, which the characters never learn. Three friends come to sit with him, say nothing for seven days, and then spend some twenty-five chapters arguing that suffering of this kind has a cause and he should admit it. Job refuses, and keeps demanding a hearing. When God finally answers out of the whirlwind, it is with questions rather than explanations — about weather, wild animals, the sea, and two creatures described at length. Job is restored at the end. He is never told why.
proverbs:
Proverbs is not one book but several collections bound together, and it helps to know which one you are in. Chapters one to nine are sustained speeches — a father to a son, and Wisdom herself personified as a woman calling in the street. From chapter ten the form changes to single couplets, hundreds of them, largely unconnected, each complete in a line. Later sections are attributed to unnamed wise men, to Agur, and to King Lemuel's mother.

One group is introduced as proverbs of Solomon "which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out" — a note about editing, three centuries after Solomon, left in the text. The sayings are general truths about how life usually goes rather than promises about how it always will; Job and Ecclesiastes are in the same Bible partly to say so. The final chapter is an acrostic poem, twenty-two verses running through the Hebrew alphabet, describing a woman who buys fields and trades and is not afraid of the snow.
jeremiah:
Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, from the reign of Josiah through the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC and into the aftermath, and almost nobody listened. He was from Anathoth, a priestly village a few miles from Jerusalem, and his own townsmen plotted against him. His message — that Babylon would take the city and resistance was futile — was heard as treason, and he was beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and lowered into a cistern for it.

The book is not in chronological order, which surprises readers who expect a narrative. It moves between oracles, sermons, biography, and passages often called the confessions, where Jeremiah complains to God in language nobody else in scripture uses. It contains the temple sermon, the potter's house, the seventy years, a scroll that Jehoiakim cut up and burned page by page, and the promise of a new covenant written on the heart. He is last seen in Egypt, taken there against his will by the people he stayed behind with.
lamentations:
Lamentations is five poems about the destruction of Jerusalem, and they are formally strict in a way that is invisible in English. Chapters one, two and four each have twenty-two verses beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter three has sixty-six — three verses per letter. Chapter five has twenty-two verses and abandons the acrostic altogether, which is the point at which the form gives way.

What it describes is siege and its aftermath: famine, the temple entered, children asking for bread, a city that was full of people sitting alone. It does not soften any of this or hurry past it. At the exact centre, in the tightest of the five poems, comes the passage everyone knows — his compassions fail not, they are new every morning — and then the lament resumes. Jewish tradition reads the whole book on Tisha B'Av, the fast that marks the day the temple fell.
ezekiel:
Ezekiel was a priest, deported to Babylon in 597 BC in the wave before the city finally fell, and he prophesied by an irrigation canal called the Chebar among other exiles. He dates his visions precisely, which makes his book one of the easiest to place in time and one of the strangest to read. It opens with a vision of a storm out of the north, four living creatures, wheels within wheels, and a throne above them.

Much of what he was told to do he had to perform rather than say: lie on one side for months, shave his head and divide the hair three ways, pack a bag and dig through a wall at dusk while people watched. Chapters eight to eleven describe the glory of God leaving the temple by stages, which is the hinge of the book. After Jerusalem falls the tone changes from warning to restoration — the shepherds, the valley of dry bones, a new heart of flesh — and it closes with nine chapters of measurements for a temple that has never been built, and a city whose name is "the LORD is there".
